children: Fair Isaac said it would not share expectations for its financial performance in the new fiscal year as it navigates changes in its pricing structure and slow mortgage demand.
The credit-score provider said it is transitioning its mortgage originations pricing structure to be tailored to the individual needs of customers, rather than a single flat fee.
The change comes as the company faces more competition from competitor VantageScore, which was recently approved to be used by government-backed mortgage lenders.
Given the pricing transition, FICO said it wouldn't share fiscal-year 2027 guidance at this time.
Shares slid 11% to $625.00 in after-hours trading Wednesday.
For the fiscal fourth quarter, FICO posted a profit of $175 million, or $8.12 a share, compared with $155 million, or $6.42 a share, a year earlier.

Profit included a $65 million accrual for a proposed settlement of an antitrust lawsuit related to FICO's credit score business. It also included a $48 million non-operating gain related to the sale of an equity investment where FICO had minority interest, and a $27 million charge related to layoffs.
FICO said in October it was cutting about 15% of its workforce.
Stripping out one-time items, adjusted per-share earnings were $11.10, ahead of the $10.69 anticipated by analysts, according to FactSet.
Revenue rose 27% to $657 million. Analysts surveyed by FactSet forecast revenue of $651.7 million.

Sales from FICO's credit score business increased 33%. Its business-facing scores segment increased sales by 39%, thanks to a higher mortgage origination scores unit price despite fewer mortgage originations.
FICO noted that the sluggish housing market is weighing on the mortgage market, keeping loan originations below historical norms.
